question: What was the total external debt of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) at the end of 2025, and how much did it grow from 2024?
answer: At the end of 2025, the total external debt of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) reached a record $9.4 trillion [B-idr2026-p027-c000]. This represented a 5.5 percent increase from the $8.9 trillion recorded in 2024 [B-idr2026-p027-c000].

1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025 Trends in External Debt, 2015–25
Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a rebound in lending from private creditors.

[B-idr2026-p035-c000 | data/9781464823558.pdf | page 35]
Figure 1.2 Creditor Composition of External Debt Stock in Low- and Middle-Income Countries, 2015–25
Almost three-fourths of total LMIC debt stock owed to bondholders was issued by public sector entities; that share increased 6.2 percent in 2025, to $1.8 trillion. The increase is even more pronounced when China is excluded: debt stock owed to bondholders increased 11.1 percent, to $1.8 trillion, and debt stock owed to commercial banks and other private creditors rose 8.3 percent, to $2.3 trillion (figure 1.3). The increase in private lending, which is highly procyclical, was correlated with this group of countries’ robust economic growth, as measured by their gross national income (GNI), which grew 6.0 percent in 2025. Through the most recent crises, decreases in debt stock from this creditor base have been associated with the 2008 financial crisis, the 2015 turbulence, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The robust 2025 economic growth of LMICs (excluding China) attracted lenders back to these economies, and many LMIC governments proved eager to borrow when international investors are willing to lend, even at elevated borrowing rates.

question: What components make up a country's total external debt?

• Public and publicly guaranteed external debt comprises long-term external obligations (maturities of over one year) of all public debtors, including debt held by the central government and by state-owned enterprises. question: How is short-term debt defined, and is it required to be reported to the Debtor Reporting System (DRS)?
answer: Short-term debt is defined as debt with an original maturity of one year or less [B-idr2026-p029-c001]. It is not covered under the reporting requirements of the Debtor Reporting System (DRS) [B-idr2026-p029-c001, B-idr2026-p129-c003]. However, most DRS reporters provide annual reports on outstanding short-term debt stocks on a voluntary basis [B-idr2026-p029-c001].

question: What is a total return swap (TRS)?
answer: A total return swap (TRS) is a financial derivative contract where one party transfers the total economic return of a reference asset—including income and changes in market value—to another party in exchange for a predetermined stream of payments, which is typically linked to a benchmark interest rate plus a spread [B-idr2026-p031-c002]. Traditionally, these instruments have been used to transfer the economic risks and returns of an asset without transferring its legal ownership [B-idr2026-p031-c002]. In the context of sovereign financing, TRS structures can combine derivative features with financing, often involving up-front funding and the pledging of assets, such as government securities, as collateral [B-idr2026-p031-c002].

Box 1.2 Total Return Swaps: An Emerging Form of Sovereign Financing
Total return swaps (TRSs) have traditionally been used in financial markets to transfer the economic risks and returns of an underlying asset without transferring its legal ownership. More recently, TRS structures have gained prominence as a form of sovereign financing, often involving up-front funding and the pledging of government securities or other assets as collateral.

How a TRS Works

A TRS is a financial derivative contract in which one party transfers the total economic return of a reference asset, including income and changes in market value, to another party in exchange for a predetermined stream of payments, typically linked to a benchmark interest rate plus a spread.

In sovereign transactions, TRS structures can combine derivative features with financing. This combination can blur the distinction between a financial derivative and conventional borrowing, and makes it important to assess the economic substance of the transaction.

Sovereign borrowers may turn to TRS arrangements when conventional market financing is unavailable, slow, or prohibitively expensive. By using government

The Growing Use of TRSs in Sovereign Financing

Since 2024, TRS arrangements have been identified in Angola, Argentina, Colombia, Nigeria, and Senegal, with financing amounts ranging from about $1.0 billion to $9.3 billion. Maturities have generally ranged from one to three years, and disclosed collateralization ratios have typically been between 133 and 198 percent. Net debt flows from official creditors to LMICs increased 7.7 percent to $83.0 billion in 2025, after an 18.2 percent decrease in 2024. As financing from the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic has continued to taper off, official creditors’ share of total long-term debt inflows decreased from 46.2 percent in 2024 to 24.8 percent in 2025. Net debt inflows from official multilateral creditors accounted for 89.4 percent of the official flows, increasing 3.8 percent to $74.1 billion in 2025. Trends in External Debt Flows, 2015–25
Net debt inflows (disbursements minus principal repayments) to LMICs grew for a third consecutive year, more than doubling in 2025 to $423.5 billion. From a maturity standpoint, short-term net debt inflows recorded a more than fivefold increase in 2025, to $89.4 billion, and long-term net debt inflows doubled, to $334.1 billion, approximately 78.9 percent of the total volume of net inflows. This increase in long-term net debt inflows was due to the return to lending to LMICs by private creditors in 2025; these creditors accounted for 75.2 percent of the total long-term component and increased their lending volume by 180.5 percent to $251.1 billion. Private net debt flows are highly procyclical in nature, and the return of private investors has been highly correlated with LMICs’ ongoing economic growth since the COVID-19 downturn in 2020. In 2025, LMIC economies, as measured by their GNI, grew 5.1 percent, to a cumulative $40.2 trillion.
